props.title: Facing Ali

sections.content: Facing Ali (2009) stands as one of boxing's most revealing documentaries, told through the eyes of 10 legendary fighters who faced Muhammad Ali in the ring. Unlike traditional boxing docs like When We Were Kings (1996), this film flips the perspective, letting Ali's opponents paint an intimate portrait of the champion. Director Pete McCormack brilliantly weaves together interviews with fighters like Joe Frazier, George Foreman, and Larry Holmes, who share raw, emotional accounts of preparing for, fighting, and often losing to Ali. Their stories reveal both Ali's supernatural boxing abilities and his psychological warfare that made him unstoppable.

sections.content: The film gains extraordinary power by focusing on fighters like Ken Norton, who broke Ali's jaw in their first fight, and George Chuvalo, who went 15 brutal rounds without being knocked down. Through their eyes, we see Ali as both showman and surgeon in the ring. One Night in Miami (2020) dramatized Ali's transformation into a cultural icon, but Facing Ali reveals his pure boxing genius through the memories of men who felt his lightning combinations firsthand. The fighters' respect, even love, for Ali decades later speaks volumes about his impact beyond the sport.

What elevates Facing Ali above standard sports documentaries is how it captures boxing's golden age through personal testimony. While The Last Dance (2020) showed Michael Jordan's dominance through game footage, this film lets Ali's opponents describe what it felt like to face perhaps the greatest heavyweight who ever lived. Their stories of training camps, pre-fight hype, and brutal exchanges in the ring provide an unvarnished look at professional boxing's most storied era. SUBHEAD: The Human Side of Boxing Legends

sections.content: The film's genius lies in how it humanizes both Ali and his opponents. George Foreman's transformation from brooding champion to Ali's close friend mirrors similar revelations in Champs (2014). Each fighter shares not just fight stories but deeply personal reflections on fame, pride, and redemption. The film becomes a meditation on aging warriors looking back on battles that defined them, similar to the touching moments in The Wrestler (2008), though here the stories are devastatingly real.
